newsitem.title: UK: WORLD BONDS - Eyes on Italy, Finland over ERM issue.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS - Eyes on Italy, Finland over ERM issue.

text.p: Italy will take centre stage as speculation builds about when the lira will re-enter the European Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM) after the Finnish markka made the move on Saturday, analysts said on Monday.

The outlook for Finnish bonds -- buoyed by the healthy state of the Finnish economy -- remains positive, with international investors set to pick up another 20 basis points in outperformance over core Bunds.
The yield spread between Italian bonds and Bunds also has potential to tighten further, they said.
"We remain bullish on Finnish bonds and expect the spread to narrow to 25 basis points in the coming months," said Juli Collins-Thompson, economist at Yamaichi International in London.
She said the 10-year Finnish bond/Bund yield spread was currently around 43 basis points.

"Although the move into the ERM was widely anticipated, Finnish bonds are likely to continue to do well reflecting investor confidence in the Finnish economy," said James Mackay, economist at PaineWebber International in London.
He said the 10-year spread against Bunds could tighten by up to 15 basis points by the end of the week.
With Finland safely on board, investors are now focusing on other possible entrants to the ERM, in particular Italy.
At 1315 GMT, December BTPs were trading at 122.84, down 44 basis points on the day.
Mackay said there may be some initial disappointment that the lira had not yet been linked to the ERM -- prompting some profit taking in Italian bonds.
But Italy's re-entry was still on the cards and expected to go ahead before the end of the year, he said.

"Around the turn of the year would be a good time for ERM re-entry," Collins-Thompson said. "That would ensure the passage of the budget and give it a good settling-in period so that a central rate against the Deutschmark can be decided."

She said the Finnish markka's entry to the ERM put pressure on Italy to enter the lira as soon as possible, but before applying for ERM membership the Italian government would want the 1997 Italian budget to be passed by the lower house.

This would confirm its fiscal plans were in place and supported by the government's communist party allies, avoiding speculation about any political pressures that could arise if things did not run as smoothly as anticipated.
Collins-Thompson said the budget would be the key concern for the Italian bond market with investors also keeping a close watch on inflation.

"There will be further spread narrowing with bouts of profit taking which are inevitable when you see a market rally like this one has," she said. "People want to take their profits and get out. But essentially we are looking for the spread to narrow to 200 basis points by the end of the year."
At 1316 GMT, the 10-year BTP/Bund yield spread was at 232 basis points, five basis points wider than Friday's 227 basis point level.
Kirit Shah, chief market strategist at Sanwa International in London, raised a note of caution, saying there was little room for further outperformance of BTPs against Bunds.
"All the good news is priced in and there isn't space to tighten beyond 200 basis points," he said.

Shah said that unlike Finland, which could meet all the fundamental criteria for European Economic and Monetary Union, Italy still had some way to go and Italian bonds would be open to potential shocks further down the road.
"Finnish entry into the ERM doesn't make a case for other countries to enter. Each country has its own domestic adgenda," he said.
